text: A window of size k slides across nums, one step at a time. Return the maximum of each window.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — for one, three, negative one, negative three, five, three, six, seven, with k equal to three, the answer is three, three, five, five, six, seven, one max per window. It's a fixed-size window, but the summary I need is the max, which is hard to maintain when the current max slides out. Are there any constraints on the input size — is n up to ten to the fifth?

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would rescan each window, which is O of n times k. A heap gets that down to O of n log k. This problem reminds me of a monotonic deque — a decreasing deque of indices. Values from front to back are decreasing, so the front is always the window max. Before pushing i, I pop from the back everything less than or equal to nums at i. They're dominated by a later, larger element and can never be the max again. Then I pop the front if it slid out of the window. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so it's amortized linear time.

To detect expiry. I need to know when the front leaves the window, which is when i minus k is at least the front index. A raw value doesn't tell me its position. I read the value back with nums at the front index.

Here's the plan, for each i. One: pop the back while nums at i is at least the value at the back. Two: pop the front while it has expired, then push i. Three: once i reaches k minus one, append the value at the front. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop over i: two while loops clean the deque, one from the back by value and one from the front by index, then I push i, and once the first full window is formed I record the front's value. One thing worth flagging — the expiry test is i minus k, greater than or equal to the front. The window covers i minus k plus one through i, so index i minus k is the first one out. Also, popping on greater than or equal, not just greater, drops equal values early — an older equal value would expire first anyway.

Let's dry-run the code. Eight, three, four, two, six, one, with k equal to three — expected eight, four, six, six. The row that matters is i equals three. The max, eight, sits at index zero, and index zero has just slid out. Popping the expired front lets four take over, so the output is four, not eight. Then at i equals four, six clears the smaller two and four from the back. It returns eight, four, six, six. That matches.
The inner while looks nested — why is it still linear?

It's amortized. Every index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the total number of pops across all iterations is at most n. It's not k pops per i — it's bounded by the total number of elements.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is O of n — each index is pushed once and popped at most once. Space is O of k — the deque holds at most one window of candidates. Oh, one more thing — mirror it with an increasing deque, and you get the sliding window minimum. The same idea, that dominated candidates are discarded, also powers monotonic-deque optimizations in dynamic programming, and prefix-sum deques.
Excellent — the front-is-max invariant, indices for expiry, the amortized argument, and the min mirror. That's a strong close.
